text: Water from a cooling tower is only as cold as the weather allows. When the mould needs it colder, you need a chiller.
Here's how it makes cold water, and how it slowly loses the ability to.
The water chiller.
A chiller doesn't make cold. It moves heat, out of the process water, and into the air outside.
It does it with a refrigerant that boils at a low temperature, running round a closed loop with four main parts.
First, the evaporator. Warm water from the moulds flows on one side of a heat exchanger. Cold, low pressure refrigerant flows on the other.
The refrigerant boils, soaking up the heat, and the water leaves colder. A common set point is seven degrees out, twelve degrees back.
Second, the compressor. It draws in the refrigerant vapour and squeezes it, so it gets hot, much hotter than the air outside.
Third, the condenser. Fans pull outside air through a finned coil. The hot vapour gives up its heat, and condenses back into a liquid.
Fourth, the expansion valve. It drops the pressure of the liquid, so it cools sharply, and meters just enough into the evaporator.
A sensing bulb on the suction line keeps a few degrees of superheat, so only vapour, never liquid, gets back to the compressor.
On the gauges, the low side tells you the boiling temperature, and the high side the condensing temperature. The gap between them is the work the compressor has to do.
Every degree that condensing temperature rises adds a few percent to the power bill.
An air-cooled chiller like this one throws its heat into the air around it. A water-cooled chiller sends it to a cooling tower instead.
But chillers rarely fail all at once. They drift.
Dust, fluff and plastic fines clog the condenser fins. Less air gets through, the condensing temperature climbs, and so do power and wear.
Sooner or later, the high pressure switch trips, usually on the hottest afternoon.
On the water side, scale and dirt foul the evaporator. The approach, the gap between water and refrigerant temperature, opens up.
A slow refrigerant leak starves the evaporator. Superheat rises, capacity falls, and the compressor runs hot.
And low water flow, from a blocked strainer or a failing pump, can freeze the water in the evaporator and split it.
Warning signs: chilled water drifting above set point at full load.
High head pressure, or a condensing temperature that climbs on a mild day.
An approach temperature creeping up against your baseline.
Bubbles in the sight glass, frost where it shouldn't be, or oil stains at the joints.
So: log pressures, temperatures and approach every shift, and watch the trend.
Clean the condenser coils on a schedule, more often in a dusty plant, and keep the air path clear.
Treat and filter the process water, and clean the strainers.
Check the fans, the electrical connections and the compressor's oil, and listen for any new noise.
Have a qualified technician leak test and check the charge, and never top up without finding the leak.
And test the flow switch and freeze protection, before the day you need them.
Clean coils. Cold water.
